summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct under its 2014 Penal Code, which extended the offence beyond Muslims to everyone, and reporting on the statute notes that death-penalty provisions remain theoretically in reach.

Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical. Police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after they were found engaging in homosexual activity in a private home. Prosecution reached into a residence on a local island, so exposure is not confined to public space or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats.

The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC. In review by the UN Human Rights Committee, the government was recommended to adopt anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and to take action against stigmatisation of homosexuals. No source in the inventory records such legislation in force.

Human-rights experts surveyed for HRMI's 2024 Maldives report most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers, as at risk of violations of empowerment rights. The same report scores political participation at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower, so the channels that function best do not include the rights on which this group depends.
tangentialFactors:
The UN OHCHR compilation for the Maldives' second-cycle Universal Periodic Review (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015) records concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage, showing the religious-law influence that also frames the criminal statute.

HRMI's 2024 expert survey groups LGBTQIA+ people with migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers as categories at risk of empowerment-rights violations, so the exposure sits within a broader pattern rather than standing alone.
localsOnly:
The Maldives government's own national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015) states that of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons, and reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years.

Residents are subject to the same Penal Code provision as visitors, and the Dhaandhoo arrests took place inside a private home on a local island, where household setting offered no protection from prosecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source addressing gender identity, legal gender recognition or trans-specific criminal provisions. The findings above rest on sexual-orientation sources, and their application to trans visitors specifically is not sourced here.

Whether the death-penalty provisions referenced in reporting on the 2014 Penal Code have ever been imposed in a same-sex conduct case is unresolved in these sources; the sourced claim is that they remain theoretically in reach.

No source in the inventory records the outcome of the Dhaandhoo prosecutions after the arrests of 29 August 2015.

Whether the Human Rights Committee's recommendation on anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation has been acted on is not recorded in the inventory.
